## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to manipulate multi-byte data with pure bitwise ops, a common low-level skill in performance-critical code.

## Key Concepts
- Byte masking with constants
- Shifts to relocate bytes
- Bitwise OR to assemble result
- No loops or branches; constant-time operation

## Code Example
```javascript
function swapBytes32(x) {
  return ((x & 0x000000FF) << 24) |
         ((x & 0x0000FF00) << 8)  |
         ((x & 0x00FF0000) >>> 8) |
         ((x & 0xFF000000) >>> 24);
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt for 64-bit values? 
- What edge cases arise in languages with signed shifts vs unsigned shifts?

## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to derive a fast, branch-conscious solution for 128-bit integers; assesses comprehension of leading-zero concept and how to extend 64-bit intrinsics to 128 bits.

## Key Concepts

- Leading zeros counting in wide integers
- 64-bit intrinsics (clz) or portable fallbacks
- Branchless or minimal-branch reasoning for performance

## Code Example

```c
int countLeadingZeros128(uint128 x){
  if (x.hi != 0) return __builtin_clzll(x.hi);
  return 64 + __builtin_clzll(x.lo);
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you implement portable clz without compiler intrinsics?
- How would you extend to 256-bit widths with identical patterns?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests a crisp bit-twiddling trick: constructing a mask anchored to the least significant set bit, plus proper zero handling.

## Key Concepts
- Isolating the LSB with n & -n
- Mask construction via (lsb<<1) - 1
- Edge-case handling for zero input

## Code Example
```javascript
function maskBelowLSB32(n) {
  const lsb = n & -n;
  return n === 0 ? 0 : (lsb << 1) - 1;
}
```

- What are the potential pitfalls on platforms with different integer sizes?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests the ability to implement a deterministic, branchless byte-level permutation on a 128-bit value, a common pattern in low-level data encoding and hash-like transformations.

## Key Concepts

- Byte slicing and reassembly
- Unrolled, fixed permutations
- Inlining and branchless bit-twiddling

## Code Example

```c
// P is a 16-element permutation of {0..15}, evaluated at compile time
uint128 permuteBytes128(uint128 x) {
  return ( (x >> (8*0)) & 0xFF) << (8*P[0]) |
         ( (x >> (8*1)) & 0xFF) << (8*P[1]) |
         ...
         ( (x >> (8*15)) & 0xFF) << (8*P[15]);
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you validate the permutation with generic tests without codegen changes?
- How would you adapt to a runtime-permutation while preserving inlining performance?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of 128-bit shifts, wrap-around logic, and edge cases where n==0. Requires a clean, branch-minimal implementation without loops.

## Key Concepts
- Bitwise rotation across 128 bits
- Handling edge cases safely (n==0, 128-n)
- Avoiding undefined shifts across boundary bits

## Code Example
```c
uint128 rotateLeft128(uint128 x, uint8 n) {
  n &= 127;
  if (n == 0) return x;
  return (x << n) | (x >> (128 - n));
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt for a language without 128-bit integers?
- How would compiler optimizations affect this implementation in real code?
